opus-5.5.text:
I think the key difference is in what each modality actually encodes. An image is ultimately a record of the physical world: pixels, light, texture. It's very rich in low-level detail, but much of that detail is redundant. If you mask out half an image, a model can often fill it in reasonably well because the structure is fairly local and predictable. So the information density, in terms of abstract concepts per unit of data, is relatively low.

Language is different. It's something humans invented over thousands of years specifically to compress and transmit knowledge. Every sentence is already a highly abstracted representation of the world. When you write "the stock market fell because interest rates rose," you're encoding causality, economics, and time in a handful of tokens. You simply can't get that from pixels without a lot of extra inference. So when a model learns to predict the next token, it's forced to model reasoning, planning, and how humans think, not just what things look like.

There's also the question of composability. Language is discrete and symbolic, so you can combine concepts in essentially unlimited ways, and you can talk about things that don't exist: hypotheticals, mathematics, the future. That gives language a kind of open-endedness. Images are bounded by what can be seen or rendered.

And from a practical standpoint, language is the interface for reasoning. Chain-of-thought, writing code, proving theorems: these are all done in a symbolic, sequential space. If the goal is something like general intelligence, the ability to think step by step and search over possibilities, then language is a much more natural substrate for that. Vision is extremely important for grounding and for interacting with the physical world, but I see it more as the perception layer, while language sits closer to cognition itself. That's why I think the ceiling is higher.

That said, I don't think it's either-or. The most interesting direction is how to let language-based reasoning connect with perception, so the model isn't just manipulating symbols but actually understands what they refer to.

r001.rationale: It says language can combine concepts in essentially unlimited ways, but does not state that speakers can define a new concept during a conversation and then refer to it by a word.

r002.rationale: It describes language as composable and open-ended, but does not state that language permits unbounded nesting.

r003.rationale: The response discusses language as a reasoning medium, but does not say that language can refer to itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key is that language is already a compressed, structured representation of the world. When humans write, we've already done a lot of the work: we've abstracted away the pixels, thrown out the noise, and kept the concepts, the causal relationships, the reasoning. So a model trained on text is essentially learning from a distillation of human thinking that took thousands of years to produce.

Images are different. An image is very high-dimensional, but most of that information is low-level: textures, lighting, exact positions of things. The semantic content, the part that actually matters for understanding, is a tiny fraction of the signal. So when you scale up an image model, a lot of capacity goes into modeling things that don't contribute much to intelligence. You get beautiful images, but the model is not necessarily learning to reason.

Language also has this property of being compositional and recursive. You can describe a procedure, then describe a procedure that modifies that procedure, and so on. You can talk about things that don't exist, about counterfactuals, about abstract math. It's very hard to express "if this assumption were false, then this theorem wouldn't hold" with pixels. But in language it's trivial. And that's exactly the kind of structure you need for planning and reasoning, which is where I think the real ceiling lies.

One more thing: language gives you a natural interface for self-improvement. A language model can write down its own reasoning, critique it, search over alternatives, verify them. The output and the input live in the same space. With images that loop is much harder to close. So from a research perspective, language is where I see the most room to keep climbing, even though images and video obviously remain very important for grounding.

r001.rationale: The response describes language expressing abstract ideas and procedures, but does not say new concepts can be defined in conversation and then referred to by a word.

r002.rationale: It describes a procedure that modifies another procedure, continuing “and so on,” which communicates unbounded nesting.

r003.rationale: It says a language model can write down and critique its own reasoning, communicating language used to refer to and operate on its own content.

astra-6.text:
I think language may have a higher ceiling because it lets us describe things far beyond what we can directly observe. An image captures a particular scene, but language can express an abstract rule, a hypothetical situation, or a relationship between things that have never appeared together in an image. You can talk about infinity, for example, even though you cannot take a photograph of it.

Language also gives us a way to build on previous knowledge. We can take a concept, give it a name, and then use it as a building block for a more complicated concept. A mathematical proof or a computer program can carry a lot of structure in a relatively short sequence of symbols.

So if you train a model to understand and generate language, the task can eventually demand more than recognizing patterns. It can demand reasoning about causes, following an argument, or working through a problem. That is where I see the potentially higher ceiling. Of course, learning to produce convincing language does not automatically mean the model can do all those things reliably.

r002.rationale: The response mentions building more complicated concepts, but does not state that language permits unbounded nesting.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that language can refer to itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language may have a higher ceiling because it can describe things that aren’t directly visible. An image gives you a very rich observation, but language can express an abstract concept, a causal relationship, or a hypothetical situation: what would happen if we changed something? You can also use language to describe how to solve a problem, step by step.

So learning language potentially means learning more than the patterns in the text. To predict what someone will say next, you may need to understand their situation, their intentions, and something about how the world works. That creates an opportunity to learn increasingly sophisticated representations.

Of course, that doesn’t mean text contains everything. Vision and interaction provide grounding that language alone may miss. But language gives us a way to build on abstractions, and then build further abstractions on top of those. That’s why I think its potential ceiling may be higher.
